newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Thousands in Gaza march for Palestinian prisoners.
newsitem.headline: Thousands in Gaza march for Palestinian prisoners.

text.p: Thousands of Palestinian protesters marched down Gaza's main street on Monday demanding Israel free their imprisoned sons and end a closure it imposed after a suicide attack last month in Jerusalem.
"As long as my son is in prison, I don't feel any peace," said a woman, whose 24-year-old son Ahmad is serving a life term in an Israeli jail.
The protesters -- including the wife of imprisoned Hamas spiritual leader Sheikh Ahmad Yassin -- cradled framed, blown-up photos of their husbands and sons and waved Palestinian flags.
"Yasser -- the leader and the president -- we are with you," one sign read, referring to Palestinian President Yasser Arafat. "There's no peace keeping prisoners as hostage," said another.

The protests coincided with a new peace mission by U.S. envoy Dennis Ross to try and save Israeli-Palestinian peacemaking which hit crisis level after two Moslem bombers killed themselves and 14 people in a Jewish market in Jerusalem on July 30.
Palestinian officials say 3,500 political prisoners remain in Israeli jails.

"No agreement should be reached in the future without the prisoners included," said Palestinian intelligence officer Ziad al-Mashrawi at the protest, which began in front of the International Committee of the Red Cross.

Israel's previous government freed more than 5,000 Palestinian prisoners under interim peace deals but froze releases after a series of Islamic militant suicide bombings killed 57 people in the Jewish state in early 1996.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who took office in June 1996, in a January deal handing over most of the West Bank town of Hebron to PLO rule agreed to free more prisoners but so far has released only Palestinian women prisoners, just a handful of the 3,500 prisoners.
In Ramallah, about 50 Palestinian youths burned tyres and tried to throw stones at Israeli soldiers following a protest against the closure.
Palestinian police entered Israeli-controlled territory to disperse the demonstrators.
In Gaza, a truck laden with homegrown produce was brought in to protest the closure, and fishermen towed in one of their boats, holding up empty nets.
Israel closed its borders to thousands of Palestinian labourers after the July 30 bombing. It also restricted travel between West Bank cities, villages and towns.

Unemployment in Arab areas has since jumped to 70 percent, with workers barred from reaching jobs in Israel and local industries firing employees for lack of supplies, according to the Palestinian Ministry of Labour.
Israel says its measures are necessary to prevent further suicide bombings.
But Palestinians condemned the closure as collective punishment, and protesters sounded a warning of an "explosion" that "nobody will be able to control" if it continued.
"If the explosion comes it will exceed Gaza, the West Bank and Israel. It will paralyse the whole region and stability will collapse," said Telecommunications Minister Imad Falouji.
